newsitem.title: BURMA: More religious strife in Burma, security tightened.
newsitem.headline: More religious strife in Burma, security tightened.

text.p: More Buddhist-Moslem troubles were reported near Rangoon on Monday as Burma's military government beefed up security in the capital around monasteries and other religious sites, witnesses and religious sources said.
More than 100 monks were detained in the capital on Sunday following several different attacks on Moslem buildings and a street demonstration, witnesses said.

A group of young Buddhist monks was detained after attacking an Islamic religious school in Thakayta, about 10 km (six miles) southeast of Rangoon late on Sunday, said Hadji U Thein, president of the Islamic Religious Affairs Council.
"The building was slightly damaged and the monks were taken away by security personnel," he told Reuters on Monday.
Another group of monks stoned a different mosque in Rangoon late on Sunday, and the people inside the mosque threw stones back in retaliation, eyewitnesses said.
Although the monks were not seen entering the mosque, security personnel took the monks away in trucks, the witnesses said. Their destination was not known.

At least four other truckloads carrying a total of about 90 monks were also seen driving into a disused horserace course in Rangoon on Sunday, witnesses said. They were rounded up after trying to hold a protest near the centre of town, the witnesses said.
The Kyaikkasan Ground has been frequently used by the government as a temporary detention centre during times of unrest.
Government officials and Buddhist authorities were not immediately available for comment on the detention or reports of unrest.
Security was beefed up near some mosques and Buddhist monasteries in Rangoon on Monday, witnesses said, as more armed troops and barricades were seen in the streets of the capital.

An 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. curfew continued in Burma's second city Mandalay where the unrest began just over a week ago, when monks went on a rampage in the city, attacking several mosques and launching street protests.
The unrest was sparked in part by reports that a Buddhist girl, said to be the niece of a monk, was raped by a Moslem.

Other sources said the demonstration and vandalism began following reports that the Buddha image at the Mahamuni pagoda -- one of the most important religious sites in Mandalay -- was vandalised and some gold or jewels were stolen.
Religious Affairs Minister Lieutenant-General Myo Nyunt urged Buddhist monks on Sunday to teach young monks good conduct and to remember to follow religious principles.
"The main purpose...is to propagate, purify and perpetuate the religion," Myo Nyunt was reported on Monday as saying in a speech to senior monks at a ceremony on Sunday.
"Please remove all obstacles that would mar propagation and perpetuation of the relgion and teach the young and your disciples to be filled with a good code of conduct," he was reported as saying.
Burma is 90 percent Buddhist and about four percent Moslem.
Its 430,000 monks play a key role in this deeply religious country and have in the past lent their support to political and social causes.
